newsitem.title: FRANCE: Police role probed in search of Paris mayor's flat.
newsitem.headline: Police role probed in search of Paris mayor's flat.

text.p: A Paris court questioned the head of the city's criminal investigation division on Monday about why he refused police aid to a judge searching the home of the capital's mayor in a corruption probe, justice source said.

A court, which decides whether to commit suspects for trial, questioned CID chief Olivier Foll over his July decision to prevent officers from helping anti-corruption judge Eric Halphen search the home of mayor Jean Tiberi in an inquiry into the finances of France's ruling Gaullist party.
Halphen ended up searching Tiberi's home on his own while Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre expressed support for Foll.
The policeman's lawyer told reporters his client withdrew officers from the case because Halphen only told them outside the building that they were going to search Tiberi's home.
Lawyer Jean-Marc Varaut said Halphen's attitude showed he mistrusted police. He also said Halphen did not follow correct legal procedures when requisitioning police for the search.

French media have alleged that Halphen feared that police officers assigned to help him reported his actions to their own superiors in order to slow investigations uncomfortably close to Jacques Chirac's office as Paris mayor before his election as president in 1995.
Foll could face legal action or be suspended if the court found he violated the law in refusing to aid the judge.
Halphen has for months been investigating allegations of kickbacks to Chirac's Rally for the Republic party in connection with housing contracts in the Paris area.
